cards.q: Do lift, weight, thrust and drag act through the same point in a real aircraft?
cards.c: No. Each force acts along its own distinct line because they originate from different parts of the aircraft.
w: Yes, all four forces intersect at the exact center of gravity
Yes, in steady flight all forces share a single common line of action
No, only lift and weight act through a single point

cards.q: Through which point does lift act, and what determines where it is?
cards.c: Lift acts through the Centre of Pressure (CP); its position depends on the position of the wings and changes with angle of attack.
w: Lift acts through the Centre of Gravity; it is fixed by total weight
Lift acts through the engine centerline; it depends on thrust setting
Lift acts through the tailplane; it depends on aircraft speed

cards.q: How does the position of the centre of pressure change?
cards.c: It changes with changes in angle of attack (alpha).
w: It remains fixed at the exact geometric center of the wing
It moves backward as speed decreases to zero
It shifts entirely to the tail when banking

cards.q: Through which point does weight act, and what does that point depend on?
cards.c: Weight acts through the Centre of Gravity (CG); it depends on weight distribution and fuel usage.
w: Weight acts through the Centre of Pressure; it depends on lift generation
Weight acts through the nosecone; it depends on payload volume
Weight acts through the propeller hub; it depends on engine power

cards.q: What decides the line of thrust?
cards.c: The position of the propeller shaft or jet engine centerline.
w: The angle of attack of the main wings
The position of the centre of pressure on the airfoil
The placement of the horizontal tailplane

cards.q: Why is the drag line the most difficult to find?
cards.c: Because drag is the combined resistance of every part of the aircraft, requiring separate estimates or wind-tunnel testing.
w: Because drag acts in the opposite direction of lift
Because drag remains constant regardless of airspeed or angle of attack
Because drag only exists when the engines are shut down

cards.q: How does drag behave as angle of attack changes?
cards.c: Drag is liable to change with changing angles of attack.
w: Drag decreases linearly to zero at high angles of attack
Drag stays completely constant during all flight maneuvers
Drag shifts instantly to the center of gravity

cards.q: In Figure 2.20, which line is higher: thrust or drag? Which is further back: lift or weight?
cards.c: Drag is higher than thrust; lift is further back than weight.
w: Thrust is higher than drag; weight is further back than lift
Both forces share identical lines of action with no offset
Thrust is higher than drag; lift is directly aligned with weight

cards.q: Why is it advantageous to place lift slightly behind weight?
cards.c: It gives a nose-down pitching tendency in the event of loss of thrust, automatically pitching the nose down into a safe glide.
w: It ensures that the aircraft climbs automatically without engine power
It eliminates the need for any tailplane or control surfaces
It makes the aircraft accelerate infinitely when thrust is increased

cards.q: Why should the drag line be above the thrust line, according to the source?
cards.c: To create a nose-up couple that counteracts the nose-down tendency of the lift-weight couple.
w: To make the aircraft roll faster during banking maneuvers
To ensure that drag aids the engine in pushing the aircraft forward
To eliminate all aerodynamic pitching moments entirely

cards.q: What is a couple, and what are the two couples in Figure 2.20?
cards.c: A couple is a pair of equal, opposite forces that do not act along the same line, producing a turning effect; the two couples are the L-W couple and the T-D couple.
w: A couple is a single force acting on two wings; the couples are lift and weight
A couple is an engine pairing; the couples are port and starboard thrust
A couple is a flight maneuver; the couples are climb and descent

cards.q: What must be true of the two opposing couples for equilibrium?
cards.c: They should be equal and opposite and cancel each other out (net force and net turning effect are both zero).
w: The lift-weight couple must be twice as strong as the thrust-drag couple
The thrust-drag couple must dominate to keep the aircraft climbing
Both couples must act along the exact same straight line

cards.q: What happens in pitch if thrust is lost in the ideal arrangement?
cards.c: The nose-down lift-weight couple is left alone, causing the aircraft's nose to drop naturally into a safe glide.
w: The aircraft immediately stalls because all lift disappears instantly
The nose-up thrust-drag couple takes over and flips the aircraft upside down
The aircraft maintains level flight indefinitely using remaining momentum

cards.q: What does the source call the arrangement of Figure 2.20?
cards.c: The ideal arrangement (or ideal disposition).
w: The balanced aerodynamic failure mode
The neutral stability configuration
The unstable divergence setup

cards.q: What provides help when the ideal arrangement is not possible?
cards.c: The tailplane (the small horizontal wing at the tail).
w: The main landing gear doors
The vertical stabilizer and rudder assembly
Extra fuel tanks mounted on the wingtips

cards.q: In Figure 2.21, what do P and G represent?
cards.c: P represents the Centre of Pressure (where lift acts), and G represents the Centre of Gravity (where weight acts).
w: P represents propeller thrust; G represents ground friction
P represents pitch angle; G represents gravitational acceleration
P represents pilot controls; G represents gravitational force

cards.q: In Figure 2.21, in which direction is the tailplane force, and what is it opposing?
cards.c: The tailplane force acts downward (or upward depending on L-W offset) and opposes the net pitching couple of the main forces.
w: The tailplane force acts forward and opposes total aircraft drag
The tailplane force acts vertically up and opposes total aircraft weight
The tailplane force acts sideways and opposes yawing moments

cards.q: Why can the tailplane be small if it is far from the centre of gravity?
cards.c: Because a tailplane far from the CG has a long lever arm, meaning a small force can create a large turning effect (moment = force * distance).
w: Because air density is much lower at the tail than at the wings
Because the tailplane produces more lift than the main wings
Because it does not experience any aerodynamic drag

cards.q: If lift is behind weight (box analogy view), which way does the tailplane force act?
cards.c: A downward force is needed at the tail to balance the nose-down tendency.
w: An upward force is needed at the tail to lift the fuselage
A sideways force is needed to counteract engine torque
No tail force is needed because the forces balance automatically

cards.q: If lift is in front of weight, which way does the tailplane force act?
cards.c: An upward force is needed at the tail to balance the nose-up tendency.
w: A downward force is needed to push the tail into the ground
A backward force is needed to slow down the aircraft
No force is needed because the aircraft is naturally unstable

cards.q: What is the job of the tailplane according to the source?
cards.c: To provide the upward or downward force necessary to counteract the behaviour of the four main forces and restore equilibrium.
w: To generate 50% of the total lift required by the aircraft
To act as the primary engine mount for twin-engine aircraft
To replace the rudder during high-speed turns

cards.q: A student says that if L = W and T = D the aircraft is necessarily in equilibrium. Correct this.
cards.c: Wrong. Balanced forces are not the same as balanced turning effects; the lines of action must also be offset/balanced to prevent rotation.
w: Right. Equal forces always guarantee complete flight equilibrium
Right, because forces completely describe all aircraft motion
Wrong, because lift must always exceed weight in level flight

cards.q: A lift-weight couple of 800 lb-ft nose-down must be balanced by a tailplane 16 ft behind the centre of gravity. What force is needed?
cards.c: Force = Moment / Distance = 800 / 16 = 50 lb (downward).
w: Force = 800 lb (equal to the couple magnitude)

cards.q: Compare the effects on pitch of lift behind weight and of drag above thrust, including the box analogy view.
cards.c: Lift behind weight acts like pulling the top of a box backward while weight pushes down, creating a nose-down moment; drag above thrust pushes the top forward while thrust pushes the bottom, creating a nose-up moment.
w: Both couples create identical nose-up pitching moments
Lift behind weight creates a nose-up moment while drag above thrust creates a nose-down moment
Both couples create nose-down pitching moments that require full engine power to cancel

cards.q: Which factors can change the centre of gravity during a flight, according to the source?
cards.c: Weight distribution and fuel usage as fuel is burned from the tanks.
w: Changes in ambient air temperature and barometric pressure
The deployment of landing gear and flaps
Variations in angle of attack and airspeed
